utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Will you please call the case, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have the appearances for today, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. Daryl Mundis, for the Prosecution, assisted by our case manager, Alma Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to our learned friends from the Prosecution. Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson representing General Delic, with our legal assistant, Lana Deljkic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness is not in court because the Defence has asked for some time to raise an important housekeeping issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It relates to Dzemal Vuckovic, who is scheduled to testify later today. Your Honours, the Defence would wish to object to the Prosecution proposal to lead the evidence of this witness pursuant to Rule 92 ter, and also we object to the manner in which the Prosecution is proposing to deal with the documents associated with that witness. If I can set out the background to this matter, and I apologise because I'll need to do so at some length. On the 19th of October of this year, the Prosecution sent a letter to the Defence, setting out a list of all the witnesses that it was proposing to call pursuant to Rule 92 ter, and the witness, Dzemal Vuckovic, was contained within in that list. At that stage, the Prosecution had disclosed a witness statement to the Defence, dated the 22nd of September, 2006, in which it referred to 21 documents. The Defence, therefore, prepared its cross-examination on the basis of that statement and also took on board the likelihood that the Prosecution would seek to admit all of those 21 documents. Now, on Friday, the 2nd of November, the Prosecution sent a further letter to the Defence, and in that letter it stated that the Prosecution had revisited its exhibit list and noticed that there were many bulletins and special information reports contained within the list. It then indicated a wish to raise or use those bulletins and special information reports in connection with the evidence of Vuckovic. In this letter, the Prosecution set out a procedure that it said it would follow. It said in calling Vuckovic, it would get him to adopt his statement. The Prosecution would ask him to describe the procedure by which the bulletins and the special information reports had been produced, and then the Prosecution would tender all of the bulletins and special information reports in a summary fashion. Now, that was on Friday morning. On Friday afternoon, the Prosecution sent a further e-mail to the Defence, setting out a provisional exhibit list for the witness Vuckovic. In the provisional exhibit list, it mentioned 117 PT documents of which 94 were these bulletins or special information reports. Now, not all of the PTs related to just one document. One of the PTs, 1910, contained a collection of around some 70 bulletins within the one PT. So, in total, all the exhibits the Prosecution were proposing to use with this witness amounted to some 2.000 pages. And as I say, the Defence were just put on notice of this on Friday. The e-mail also said that the witness wished to make changes to his original witness statement, and, therefore, the Prosecution proposed to prepare a new consolidated witness statement dealing with the changes and also touching upon the new documents that the Prosecution wished to have admitted into evidence. That was the state of play on Friday. Now, on Saturday evening, after 7.00, the Prosecution sent a new consolidated statement for Mr. Vuckovic. It's a 30-page document and, in many respects, rewrites that witness's original statement. A lot of the content within that document -- within the original document has been struck out or amended. I should also say that this document was only sent in the English language as well. Within this new document, it referred to some 92 new documents that were not mentioned in the original witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me understand. An additional 92 to the about 187 that you got, 117 plus 70 within one PT that you got Friday afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: On Friday afternoon, Defence received notice the Prosecution wished to use 117.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And in one of the PTs, there were 70 pages, so it was about 187.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: There were 70 documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Seventy documents, yes. So there are about 187. Now the 90 that you are mentioning now is in addition to the 187?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It was included within the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: -- 187, yeah. Also within the new statement, there is a table in which the Prosecution has set down a brief description of what some of these PTs purport to be about, and some of those -- some of those descriptions are erroneous. So, Your Honour, that's the background to this matter. So having set that out at length, it is the Defence's submission that the Prosecution should not be permitted to call this witness pursuant to Rule 92 ter, nor to simply tender these documents and have them admitted in a summary fashion, and we rely upon a number of reasons for that. The first, as is probably no surprise to you, is that essentially the Defence has not had time to prepare properly for this witness. As I mentioned earlier, the Defence initially prepared on the basis of the original statement. It's now received, as I say, some 2.000 new pages at a very, very late stage. The document, the new statement, has only been disclosed in English. I can inform you that last night, at 9.39, a B/C/S version of the statement was disclosed to the Defence. The consequence, of course, is that the Defence has not been able to take proper instructions from General Delic on the contents of this statement, nor the documents which it's been proposed -- the Prosecution is proposing to use. Now, what I would like to remind the Trial Chamber of is a decision that was issued in September, because it's my submission that this is ground that the Trial Chamber has been over before, previously. If you recall, in September, the Prosecution filed a motion in which it sought to admit the evidence of three witnesses and in which it simply wished to tender the exhibits of those witnesses which were referred to in their witness statements, and the Trial Chamber issued a decision on the 27th of September in which it rejected that approach. In that decision -- and I should say that in respect of that Prosecution motion in September, it was also an 11th-hour motion in which the Prosecution had not disclosed statements and documents in the B/C/S language. The Trial Chamber held that, with such a late application, risks endangering the right of an accused to a fair trial arose. It also held that such an approach impacts upon any expeditiousness which may have been gained from the use of Rule 92 ter, as the Defence was unable to properly prepare for cross-examination. And, thirdly, the Trial Chamber held that it was not in the interests of justice to allow the Prosecution to proceed using the Rule 92 ter procedure with such an approach. In my respectful submission, Your Honours, we have a very, very similar situation here again; 11th-hour application, documents not disclosed in the B/C/S language. And, similarly, as with the earlier decision, it's my submission that it would not be in the interests of justice to enable or permit the Prosecution to take such an approach. The second argument I wish to raise is that the Prosecution is seeking to introduce a very substantial amount of evidence onto the trial record without any proper scrutiny or any process to determine whether there is a proper basis to admit that evidence. In the Trial Chamber's decision of the 27th of September, the Trial Chamber pointed out the importance of the guidelines on admission and presentation of evidence and conduct of counsel in court in this regard. In that decision, the Trial Chamber pointed out that in paragraph 18 of those guidelines, a party calling a witness will be permitted to show documents to a witness during the direct examination of a Rule 92 ter witness, and such documents may be tendered into evidence; in other words, it made it clear that if a Rule 92 ter witness came, any attempt to tender documents through that witness should be done as a separate part during the viva voce stage. The decision also emphasised the importance of a party demonstrating a relation between the witness and the document being proposed to be admitted into evidence. In my submission, Your Honours, if the Prosecution are permitted to introduce documents in such a summary fashion, the normal process by which the Trial Chamber can scrutinize each document before it's entered onto the record, to ensure that only relevant documents go onto the record, is lost. Also, the Defence will lose the opportunity to confront each and every document as it is brought up in court. Thirdly, Your Honours, as I've mentioned, the new statement of Mr. Vuckovic refers to an enormous amount of documents, and I would remind the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution of the guidance given by the Trial Chamber on Friday, the 26th of October, and that was in relation to the first Rule 92 ter witness that the Chamber heard. And on that occasion, His Honour Judge Harhoff emphasised to the Prosecution that if they wanted to have documents admitted through a Rule 92 ter witness, then it should only be a small number of documents. Judge Harhoff mentioned that he had in mind one or two documents. Your Honour, Judge Moloto, you emphasised to the Prosecution that the purpose of the Rule 92 ter exercise is it should save time, and you pointed out that you might save time on the leading side, but the result could be that you're expanding it on the cross-examining side. So essentially, in my submission, that's what we're looking at here today. Finally, Your Honours, just to close on this point, and this is really more an observation: This witness is an important witness, and what the Defence would point out is that it would seem that the Prosecution are seeking to use this approach of calling witnesses through the Rule 92 ter procedure, tendering a lot of documents, new documents, through that witness, and they are reserving this approach for the most important witnesses or certainly some of the most important witnesses. This is an approach that we, in principle, object to. Now, it's obviously a matter to the Prosecution as to how they conduct their case, but it's the Defence's belief that the Prosecution should really be calling these important witnesses viva voce; and if there are important documents to be put through these witnesses, then that should be done during live testimony rather than adducing or seeking to tender these documents in this summary fashion that will not allow for proper scrutiny of the documents before they're admitted into the trial record. Your Honour, the remedy that I'm seeking today, in conclusion, is that the witness should be called viva voce rather than being called pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robson. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll be extremely brief, as my colleague Mr. Neuner has been dealing with this witness and is obviously not in the courtroom at the moment. As a starting point, let me perhaps just briefly offer the Trial Chamber a proffer of what Mr. Vuckovic will testify about, because I believe that that sets forth relevant information that Your Honours need with respect to this issue. This witness worked in the Security Administration and was the person who was in charge of compiling the security bulletins. We've seen a small number of those documents here in court. This witness received information reports from subordinate units, including the corps, the various corps, took those information reports, analysed and compiled them, and created the security bulletins. He is, in effect, the author of a large number of these security bulletins which are on the Prosecution exhibit list. However, this witness is not in a position to testify about the underlying events described in those documents. He is, in effect, the compiler of the information that he receives. He compiled the information, he did some analytical work, he reduced the scope of some of those incoming reports, perhaps, and created the bulletins. He's not going to be in a position, my understanding is, at least from speak to go Mr. Neuner. My understanding is that the witness will not be in a position to comment about the accuracy of the information he received, about the sources of the information that he received, et cetera. He is, in effect, similar to a witness who would be an archivist, for example. Someone who would say, "I created these bulletins," or, "Information came in to me, I compiled the information, I forwarded it along." He's not going to be in a position where he's going to have independent knowledge about each and every thing that was written in those security bulletins. So, in effect, the purpose of what he's going to be testifying about is simply how the bulletins were created and what he did with them. That is the limit of his testimony with respect to the bulletins. The more over-arching point, however, which goes to the issue of the Defence challenge to the use of Rule 92 ter, let me briefly state, I'm not sure that the Defence has standing to even raise that issue. The Defence should not be in a position to tell the Prosecution how to lead its case. We have chosen to use the 92 ter procedure for a number of witnesses. Those witnesses have been identified to the Defence, and it is certainly well within the Prosecution duties and responsibilities to put the evidence before the Trial Chamber that the Trial Chamber needs in order to reach the ultimate decisions on this case. The means and methods by which we do that, as long as they conform to the Rules and the Statute, is a matter for the Prosecution. Let me indicate that in this type of situation, the obvious remedy would be if the Defence requires additional time for cross-examination, so be it. It's very clear, given the timing, that it's extremely unlikely that Mr. Vuckovic would commence cross-examination today under any circumstance; and if the Defence certainly needed more time to prepare him, obviously we're not sitting tomorrow, and they'll have adequate time between today and Wednesday afternoon, when we sit, to prepare for cross-examination. All of the bulletins and special information reports that have been referred to by my learned colleague, Mr. Robson, were on the Prosecution exhibit list. It's not like these documents simply appeared Saturday at 7.00 in the evening. They were all on the exhibit list. They've all been disclosed. What we have simply done is updated the exhibit list with adequate notice to the Defence. I will tell the Trial Chamber, with respect to some of the time issues Mr. Robson raised, Mr. Neuner met with this witness for several hours on Friday afternoon. He met with the witness for more than ten hours on Saturday. All of these bulletins were gone through by the witness. The new 30-page statement, that Mr. Robson refers to, we produced and disclosed to the Defence and the Chamber's legal officers, a redline version, so the Defence could see exactly what was deleted, what was added, and what was changed. More than ten of those 30 pages are simply a table that describes all of the bulletins that the witness was shown. My understanding, from speaking to Mr. Neuner, is that in a conversation with Mrs. Vidovic, it was decided that the descriptions, which Mr. Robson has indicated contain some erroneous information, those descriptions are being removed from the final version of the statement. The witness, this morning or today, is meeting -- actually, as I speak, is meeting with Mr. Neuner, going through the Bosnian language version of the statement which was translated and disclosed late last evening, in order to sign the Bosnian language version of the statement without the erroneous descriptions in the accompanying table. We are doing everything we possibly can to comply with the Rules and to comply with the time limits that the Trial Chamber has imposed upon the Prosecution, and this procedure that we have proposed with respect to this witness and perhaps other witnesses certainly complies with the Rules and, in our respectful view, is a matter for the Prosecution in terms of how we present our case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps if I could just respond to two points raised by my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis has suggested that the proper remedy for this situation is to allow more time for Defence to cross-examine the witness. With respect, Your Honours, that would not solve the situation. The problem is that it's the late disclosure of this material, and the real issue is the Defence has not had proper time to prepare and take instructions, and that is something that will not be remedied by giving Defence additional time to cross-examine this witness. The second point I would say, Your Honour, is that it's been suggested that the Defence may not have standing to make this objection. I'd refer the Trial Chamber back to a discussion that took place several weeks ago when the idea of using Rule 92 ter witnesses was first brought up, and the Defence on that occasion said that we would, in each instance, reserve the right to object if we thought it appropriate. If the Defence sees a situation where the Prosecution are not conforming with the spirit of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and the rights of the accused and the Statutes are jeopardised, we will object each and every time. Finally, Your Honours, just to say that there are more witnesses to come. There are more witnesses the Prosecution are proposing to call under Rule 92 ter, important witnesses. We don't have the exhibit lists for those witnesses, and we are certainly bringing this problem to the Trial Chamber's attention because we don't want this issue to arise each and every time there's an important Rule 92 ter witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, two questions I would like to raise with you. In your address, you said you gave adequate notice to the Defence, and what do you mean by "adequate notice"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In terms of the exhibits to be shown to the witness, that was done on Friday, and I believe that that complies with the Trial Chamber guidelines with respect to two days of notice with respect to the exhibits. That's what I was referring to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Tell me, the exhibits that you show two days before you come to court, are they not the exhibits that are listed in the 65 ter list of which you gave long-time notice?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. I mentioned that earlier, that certainly all of the documents we're talking about are on the exhibit list, which was filed more than a year ago. All of these documents were disclosed to the Defence a year ago, more than a year ago. What we're simply talking about are the documents to be shown to this witness, and the Defence was put on notice about those documents on Friday. And as I've indicated, it's unlikely that the cross-examination will begin today, anyway, so the Defence will certainly have until Wednesday at 2.15 to review that material with respect to the specifics of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. My second question to you is: What are these information reports intended to show, so many of them? If this witness has got no personal knowledge of the contents and he's just giving us an explanation of how he compiled these documents, why can't that be shown, demonstrated with one copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, it could be, Your Honour, and that's precisely why Mr. Neuner and the Prosecution team have proposed doing this in a summary fashion; in other words, we're not proposing to sit down with this witness and have him flip through a large binder, which is what we're talking about, and indicate that each and every one of those documents was created by him. He's done that in the statement. The written statement refers to each and every one of these bulletins. He will then, perhaps, be asked to explain how they were created, how he compiled them, and verify that, in fact, all of those documents were created in the manner in which he has said that they were. The contents, certainly, is a question of weight that the Chamber may give to those documents in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think we are at cross-purposes. My question was: If he is to tell us how he compiled these documents, why can't the Prosecution tender one copy of those documents, of those reports, instead of tendering a whole either 94, 117, 187 of them in summary form, because he is not speaking to the contents of these documents anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That is correct. He is, however, the author of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The documents contain information about the El Mujahedin Detachment. They contain information about incidents involving that unit. They contain a wide range of references to the El Mujahedin Detachment, and that's why each and every one of the documents that have been selected are important and relevant to this case. It's not a question of one of the documents; it's a question of a series of documents over a period of time where the El Mujahedin Detachment is discussed or incidents involving that unit are discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, can I just put a couple of questions in extension of what the Presiding Judge has already asked you. First of all, I point to our guidelines, which you referred to yourself, and I think the idea with the guidelines was that the other party should be given two working days' notice before the start of the testimony for that other party to read and study the documents. Now, it doesn't seem to me that this requirement is fulfilled if you notify the other party Friday evening for the witness to testify Monday morning. That's my first question. My second question relates to your interpretation of Rule 92 ter, and this, mind you, has been the subject of discussions and exchange of views several times during this trial. I cannot claim that I have any authoritative interpretation of this Rule, but my own understanding of the Rule is that there is and there should be limits as to the number of documents that can be tendered through a 92 ter witness, simply because the purpose of the Rule lies in the possibility of not having to examine in chief the witness but let his statement come in as a replacement of the examination-in-chief, and then some documents may be admitted through that way. But to imagine or to claim that the Rule 92 ter procedure would enable any party to tender as many as 2.000 pieces of paper, I think, is clearly beyond what was contemplated by Rule 92 ter. I'm not sure, even if you look at it from a broader perspective, that it is meaningful to just load all the evidence you have on the Judges' table, simply because there are limits even as to what the Judges can digest; and so, therefore, we would expect each party to carefully select the evidence that includes material of probative value which is relevant to the indictment. And, so, unless you tell us that all of these extra bulletin reports, each of them, does include material about the activities of the El Mujahid Detachment and the other Mujahedin groups, which is the basis of the indictment, then I would be reluctant to accept all of these extra bulletin reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, let me respond to the guidelines with respect to the working-day issue. I do accept that, and as I've indicated, this witness is not likely to start cross-examination until Wednesday at any rate, given the amount of time that we've spent on this issue and the fact that Mr. Sehic still has to finish his direct examination and be cross-examined, and then Mr. Neuner would conduct a limited direct examination of Mr. Vuckovic. I think that's about as far as we're going to go today, at any rate. With respect to the Rule 92 ter procedure and documents, let me, as a general rule, indicate that I believe, with all due respect, Your Honour, that there is going to continue to be a matter of disagreement about the number of documents we can tender through a 92 ter witness. The Prosecution position is that a 92 ter witness is no different than any other witness with respect to exhibits; and, simply, we -- our position is that if we need to show a witness five exhibits or ten exhibits or twenty exhibits, we can do that whether the witness is viva voce or 92 ter. That's certainly the Prosecution's position. With respect to what's been indicated as 2.000 documents, that's not exactly right. It's perhaps 2.000 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But the fact of the matter is that my team has gone through each and every one of the bulletins and there is, in fact, relevant material in each and every one of the documents that has been selected and which were shown to this witness. That's not to say that each and every one of the 2.000 pages has relevant material. I don't believe that's the case. Some of these are 10- or 15-page bulletins of which perhaps one paragraph or even one sentence might be of relevance and probative value, because the bulletins contain information on all of the corps. So, in terms of Defence time for preparation, they really need to focus their attention on those sections concerning information relating to the 3rd Corps. Material about the 1st, 2nd, 4th, 6th, 7th Corps are not really of relevance to this case. So it's -- from within those numerous bulletins, there is certainly relevant material which has probative value contained in each and every one of the documents. That's precisely why they were selected, and that's exactly why they were put on the exhibit list in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just in response to your interpretation of the guidelines, I think that the guidelines do require each of the parties to submit the lists of documents two working days before the start of the testimony, and this goes regardless of how many days it may then last until the other party gets a bite, comes to the point of cross-examining. So I think your interpretation of the guidelines is not completely in line with the spirit in the guidelines. As to your second question -- or second answer about the correct understanding of what Rule 92 ter allows a party to do in terms of admission of documents, I guess we'll have to hand down a ruling on that, so as to specify the way in which this Chamber understands the Rule. Maybe the time has come where the Chamber should hand down such a ruling, but I shall have to confer with my fellow Judges about this issue. In any case, if you have been able to identify, out of those many bulletins reports, a few places in each where you have relevant evidence about the El Mujahid Detachment and the Mujahedin groups, I think it would fall upon your shoulders, then, to direct the Chamber's and the Defence Counsels' attention directly to these, which will perhaps enable us to have a better look, rather than having to read all the 2.000 pages and find for ourselves the few places that you have identified. I would like you, as a courtesy to the Bench, to continue to do so also in the future, not only to notify the Defence of which paragraphs or sentences that you are referring to, but also to do so to the Bench, because we are, in the end, the recipients of your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. With respect to -- let me start, then, in order to correct the two-day rule, the Prosecution will not call Mr. Vuckovic today. We will commence his direct examination on Wednesday, which should cure the "two working day" problem that has arisen with respect to the announcement of his exhibits. My colleague, Mr. Neuner, indicates he will be in a position to indicate precisely which paragraph or sentence or page of each of the bulletins is directly relevant. I believe that will take him until tomorrow morning in order to do, but we will certainly disclose that in the form of most likely a table, indicating precisely which page, paragraph, or sentence is particularly relevant and probative to these issues, and that will be disclosed as soon as it is available both to the Defence and to the Chamber's legal staff. I believe, as I've indicated, Mr. Neuner tells me that will take him the most of the rest of today and into tonight in order to have that accomplished, and we'll have that disclosed tomorrow morning to the Defence and to the Trial Chamber. I should also just use this opportunity, however, to again telegraph an issue that we have raised on several prior occasions, particularly when this issue comes up, and that goes to the issue of a motion to tender documents from the Bar table. We are in the position or in the process of compiling such a motion. I would hope it would be available within the next seven to ten working days. I will indicate, as a starting point, with respect to this witness and these bulletins, that in the event the Prosecution is unable to get these documents into evidence through this witness, who again is the author of these documents, I am certainly putting the Defence on notice right now that these bulletins will be among those which we will be tendering from the Bar table in the future, in the event we're not able to use this procedure with respect to this witness. So our position is it's much better for the Defence to have the author of the documents and be in a position to cross-examine him as to how the material, how the bulletins were created, rather than to have those documents be the form -- be submitted in the form of a motion from the Bar table based upon the witness's testimony as to how they were created.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the French translation. Mr. Mundis, I find myself in a conundrum here. If this witness is unable to testify to the contents of the reports, which I understand he will be, I mean, he will be unable to testify about the correctness of the information included in these reports, then what is the purpose for the Defence to cross-examine him on the contents? As far as I understand, but I may be wrong - and please tell me so if I am - as far as I understood, the only thing this witness can testify to is whether or not that information was passed on to General Delic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point, I'm going to defer to Mr. Neuner, who, as I've indicated, has spent more than 12 hours discussing these documents with the witness and is in a much better position than I am to inform the Trial Chamber about what the witness can say with respect to each and every one of the bulletins.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I tried to explain what the witness may do without intending to testify about the witness's position, but I just try to give an indication about the witness's position in the system. In essence, what I have learned the last days spending with the witness is that he is, as part of the Security Administration of the General Staff, subordinated to Mr. Jasarevic, the head of that Security Administration. Incoming documents, for example, relevant to this trial coming from the 3rd Corps were then, as the witness told me, divided by Mr. Jasarevic to the different sections within the Security Administration, including to his section, the Analysis Department. He, as head of the Analysis Department, had, so to speak, the first grip on documents from the 3rd Corps, for example, and was within his Analysis Department then assigning the analysis of these documents to certain people working for him. So these people then wrote an analysis about the incoming reports from the 3rd Corps, for example, and later on proposed to him that these portions out of the document are relevant to be included into a bulletin which went to Mr. Delic and other members, such as the president of the Presidency, such as the prime Prime Minister, the Minister of Defence, and so on. So it was not possible to include information into the bulletin without this witness having it assigned before an analyst, without the witness getting the proposal from the analyst back, and proving that, so to speak, the information proposed would go into the bulletin. So, while the witness may not have had the -- may not have done, himself, the analysis, he was certainly in-depth involved in the selection process, in the process of approving that a certain amount of information went into a bulletin. I hope this helps to understand the importance of the witness. He can, out of this position, probably also make a comment about a certain portion, if Your Honours or if the Defence wishes to cross-examine him on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We're going to take a break and come back. We will reconvene in a short while. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Paragraph 20 of the Guidelines on Admission and Presentation of Evidence and Conduct of Counsel in Court states: "Barring exceptional circumstances, with the leave of the Trial Chamber, the parties may not tender into evidence lengthy documents such as books where only portions thereof are relevant to the evidence of the witness through whom the document is tendered; rather, when seeking the admission into evidence of such documents, be it during examination-in-chief, cross-examination, or re-examination, each party is requested to specify which portions of the document it seeks to have admitted. Each tendering party is also requested to submit electronic versions of the portions of the documents sought to be admitted." The Chamber is of the view that this is an exceptional circumstance, and the exceptional circumstance is there in the fact that these documents are intended to be tendered not for the truthfulness of their content but for proofing a particular pattern. This witness, therefore, in the Chamber's understanding of the purpose for which he is being called, cannot be cross-examined on the content, but can be cross-examined on what he did with the documents. It does not seem to be extremely necessary, therefore, to know exactly what is in the documents themselves; and even if we do know, that's not what this witness can talk about. For that reason, the Chamber feels that the documents may and can and should be admitted through the 92 ter procedure. Judge Harhoff wants to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I was having difficulties with the Prosecution's interpretation of Rule 92 ter, and so I used the break to study the history of that particular provision in our Rules. I want to, for the record, say that my understanding was perhaps not quite correct, because I have been able to ascertain that when Rule 92 ter was introduced about a year ago, there was no understanding of any formal limit as to the number of documents that could be admitted through this procedure. Still, I do have difficulties with the way in which crucial evidence is admitted through the application of Rule 92 ter. This goes to the number of the documents; although, I realise that there is no formal limit to the number of documents in the history of Rule 92 ter. It also goes to the nature of the witness, and it goes to the directness of the evidence that is being introduced, because I would have preferred, somehow, if the evidence that is contained in these reports could be introduced in a more direct manner. The reason I go along with the decision, and I do, is that, as the Presiding Judge outlined very clearly in his handing down of the decision, is that these is, indeed, exceptional circumstances. The exceptional circumstance, as far as I see it, is that there is no other way in which this evidence could be introduced, because even if we were to use Rule 65 ter and have this witness examined as a viva voce witness, we would be facing the same problem; namely, that he could not testify to the truthfulness and the accuracy of the information included in these reports. So we would not be helped by using any other procedure. For that reason, I will go along with the decision that we will admit these documents by way of Rule 92 ter; but, as the Presiding Judge also said, of course, in the end, we will only look at the paragraphs that will be identified by the Prosecution. So it's an admission with a caveat. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Just to make a formal rendering, then, the objection is overruled. The Prosecution is allowed to tender the documents through 92 ter, provided, of course, that they follow paragraph 20 of the guidelines; that is, identifying the specific parts that they want shown. Thank you very much. Can we call the witness now. Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just to take advantage of the time while the witness is being brought in, I mentioned this to my learned colleagues from the Defence, the Prosecution has now replaced the Krcmar statements with redacted versions of the statements. Those original statements were marked for identification as 642, 643, and 644. The redacted versions have now been substituted for the unredacted versions. The redacted versions are now in e-court; and, consequently, the Prosecution would move for the admission of 642, 643, and 644, which were previously marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any comment from the Defence on that point?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then the specific MFI documents are admitted into evidence, and they are marked as exhibits according to their respective numbers. Thank you very much. Good morning, sir. Sorry, we didn't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to explain why we didn't call you at 9.00, we had some housekeeping problems to sort out before we could call you. I hope you didn't feel very lonely while you waited. Let me just remind you that you are still bound by the declaration that you made at the beginning of your testimony yesterday - I beg your pardon, it was on Friday - to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Okay. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sehic.

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When we left off last week, sir, we were talking about what you had observed in Kesten on 11 September 1995 at or about 1330 hours, when you arrived there. Can you tell the Trial Chamber, sir, the approximate number of prisoners or detained persons that were present in Kesten on that day at that time?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Around 50. I'm not sure, but I would say around 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how many soldiers from your battalion or from your -- yeah, from the 5th Battalion of the 328th Mountain Brigade were present at that time?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that in the general sector of Kesten village, there were about a hundred soldiers altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how many soldiers of the 2nd Company of the 5th Battalion were in Kesten, in the village of Kesten, or in the hamlet of Kesten itself, at that time?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's what I meant when I said "a hundred." I meant a hundred men from the 2nd Company. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But my question, sir, is: How many of them did you observe in the village of Kesten when you arrived on the 11th of September, 1995?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At first, I saw a dozen of them in the vicinity of the hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber, sir, what happened to these prisoners or detained persons shortly after your arrival?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: These detained Serb soldiers had been kidnapped by the Arabs and other soldiers of the El Mujahid. I believe they were all Arabs, but I don't know which unit they belonged to, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What do you mean by "kidnapped," sir?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The Arabs took them by force from the army, i.e., from the 2nd Company that had originally captured these soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe, sir, the situation by which, as you put it, the Arabs took them by force from the army?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't give you any details of that event. When I arrived at Kesten, they had already surrounded them. A majority were already outside, almost all of them actually, and some 20 Arabs, or maybe even more, had surrounded their group. And as far as I could understand, an Arab who could also speak Bosnian said that those were their captives, but my deputy, Muhamed Omerasevic, tried to explain to him that those were soldiers that had been captured by the 2nd Company. But since the Arabs outnumbered us, we could not protect them, and the Arabs, very soon after that, took them away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sehic, when you say "took them away," can you tell the Trial Chamber whether any of the prisoners or detainees remained in Kesten after the Arabs took them away?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Two children, two civilians, remained in Kesten. None of the soldiers remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Who were these two children, these two civilians, as you put it? Who were these people?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how old these children were?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Fifteen and 17, or maybe 14 and 17 approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What happened to those two individuals?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I took the two children with me and put them in a van. My deputy was in the van. He returned to the command post with me. I drove them in the direction of the command post. En route, in the village of Marici, I came across a patrol of the military police. I pulled over and handed the two children over to them, since they were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, let me focus your attention back on the group of persons taken away by the Arabs. Can you tell the Trial Chamber about that group of persons taken away, in terms of their gender and ages?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: All the prisoners were male, and the ages ranged between 20 and 50, at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than these male prisoners, did the Arabs take away anyone else?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: After the Arabs took this group of persons away, did you ever see that group again?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you, at any point after the Arabs took the group away, see any of the Arabs who had taken the persons away again?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Probably not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe whether you observed anything as you left in the van with the two persons you've described as children? Did you pass through any villages on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I passed through the village of Krcevine, where I saw a group of soldiers. It seemed to me that they may have been those prisoners, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Trial Chamber what you meant by "a group of soldiers" that you observed in the village of Krcevine?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As I was passing through the village of Krcevine in my van, I was some 50 metres away from the spot where I saw the group standing with their backs facing me. I -- the thought occurred to me that they might be those very prisoners, but I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: After handing over the two, as you've called them, children to the military police in Marici, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I went to the command post. I ordered the assistant commander for Moral Guidance to draft a report and to send it to the Moral Guidance organ of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than this step that you took, sir, what steps, if any, did you take to brief the commander of the 328th Mountain Brigade, Mr. Zilkic, on what you had observed in Kesten?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I went to the forward command post of Commander Zilkic right away and reported to him on all the events at Kesten. It was a verbal report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say, sir, that you did this "right away," do you recall the approximate time and date that you orally reported this to Commander Zilkic?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 11th of September, at around 1600 hours, 1600 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What concerns, if any, did you have at the time the Arabs took this group of prisoners away?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: All the orders we received from the superior command contained an item specifying what was to be done with persons captured and with war booty. The soldiers who did the military part of the task would be rewarded, i.e., certain incentives would be applied. I explained the details to the commander, i.e., that the soldiers of the 2nd Company took the persons prisoner and that they ought to have been rewarded for it, as had the commanding officers who were there. However, they took the prisoners away, thus depriving the soldiers of the benefits that were due to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, Mr. Sehic, whether at that time, on 11 September 1995, you had any concerns about the safety or well-being of the persons being taken away by the Arabs?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At that point in time, no, not in particular, because the Arabs themselves had had quite a few prisoners. I thought that they would use the prisoners to exchange them for their own who had been captured or that they would use these prisoners to receive the benefits that were, in fact, due to the 2nd Company men. Those were my thoughts at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What do you mean, sir, by you thought that they might use these prisoners to receive the benefits that were, in fact, due to the 2nd Company men?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The benefits were rewards, incentives, citations, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever come to learn, Mr. Sehic, what happened to the group of prisoners taken away from Kesten on 11 September 1995 by the Arabs?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Officially, no, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What about unofficially?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Initially, there were stories to the effect that they had been exchanged. There were various stories collating, misinformation and disinformation. It's quite difficult to say what these stories were now, more than 12 years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you ever recall, sir, whether this group of prisoners was ever discussed at any briefings that you attended within the 328th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Perhaps, in the days shortly following that period, to my question as to what was going to happen to the soldiers of the 2nd Company who had done that task, whether they would be rewarded or not, the commander responded that he didn't know what was going to happen because he didn't know whether the prisoners had been exchanged or not, which meant that the commander himself did not have any information, and the same was true for his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask now that the witness be shown Exhibit 646. That's Exhibit 646.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Sehic, do you see the document on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could go to the original, the second page of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, what this document is?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is a list of captured Serb soldiers, drafted by my assistant for Security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And who was the assistant for Security?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. Izet Karahasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know when Mr. Karahasanovic drafted this document and where?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think it was written on the 11th of September, after 1300 hours, in the village of Kesten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, at the very top line, we see a date and the time. Do you know who made those markings on this document?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The date was written by Mr. Karahasanovic; whereas, I added the time at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say, sir, that this is a list of captured Serb soldiers, where were these Serb soldiers captured?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I don't know where. Perhaps they were exchanged. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What happened to the people who were listed on this document?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't understand. Can you be more specific about what happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Earlier today, sir, you described how the Arabs took a group of persons away. Are these the same persons or different persons, or do you not know the answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think those were the same persons, and I mean the ones on the list here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can we go, please, to the first page of the document, the original. I should just inform the Chamber that when these were ERN'd, the documents were ERN'd in the incorrect order, which is why the pages were like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, again, I ask you if you could carefully look at this document and tell the Trial Chamber whose handwriting appears on this page of the document.

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The list of Serb soldiers was written by Karahasanovic. Whatever I added to the text, I underlined.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, that was -- when you made a reference to text that you underlined, that was when you were interviewed by an investigator of the Tribunal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask, if the usher could assist, if the witness could be provided with an electronic pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you, sir, to underline any text on this page which you wrote, personally.

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sehic, I'm going to ask you, sir, about this part that you've underlined, which is the part that you, yourself, wrote. Do you recall when and where you were when you made these handwritten markings on this document?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I made these additional notes as soon as I learned the information. It was at a later stage, not contemporaneously. I made some annotations even after the war, in 1997 perhaps. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you take us through, sir, the text of what's written after the name of the person listed next to number 51? Can you tell us what that refers to?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: "Four, Arabs took away right away," is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes. Can you tell us what that refers to, "Four were taken away by the Arabs"?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At first, Company Commander Sogolj informed me that the Arabs had taken away four prisoners right away; however, they handed these four prisoners to the soldiers of the 2nd Corps to use them as help to pull out seriously-wounded or killed soldiers. I'm not sure. Subsequently, I learned that the four Serb soldiers were exchanged, but I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, when and where these four prisoners were handed over to the 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the general sector of Kesten, on the very day, the 11th of September, at around 1400 or 1500 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, the next line, can you read that out and describe what that refers to, please?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the group of prisoners, there were three women, too, who the security officer separated from the men and sent them, together with the courier, to the command post of Marici. Later on, I came to know that one of the women had been called "Slobodanka," but this is all second-hand information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, who told you that one of them was named "Slobodanka"?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was probably the assistant for Security or some of the soldiers. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What about the next line?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: "Two soldiers killed." These were killed Serb soldiers lying on the roadside in the Kesten area. I don't know if they are among the persons listed here. Probably not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know the circumstances under which these two Serb soldiers were killed by the roadside?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, neither the time nor the circumstances. I think that they had been killed probably before the other ones surrendered, since they were lying by the roadside. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you inquire about what had happened to them from any soldiers of your unit who were present?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What, if anything, were you told after you made these inquiries?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Before the soldiers entered the village of Kesten, they had been killed. They must have been killed during the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, what the next line on this document refers to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just interrupt. Had there been fighting in the village of Kesten, sir, at that time on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. There was fighting in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Sehic, can you look, then, at the next line on this document and tell us what that's about?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: "Two children released." Those were the two children I drove in a van. They were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what about the next line on the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is one of the two who was from Miljevici, and later on we learned that he lived somewhere around Kotorski.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say, sir, "this is one of the two," what are you referring to? What two are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Two lads, two civilians who were in the van and who were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in the first line of this subcategory, there appears a name. Do you see that name, sir?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How did you obtain that name?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that the lad told me what his name was in the van, and that he told me he hailed from Miljevici or Podvolujak. I'm not sure. I wrote that earlier on; and after perhaps two or three years, I wrote that he was living in Kotorski.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, what Mr. Karahasanovic did with this list after he compiled it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think he submitted it to the security organs of the 328th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask now that the witness be shown the document previously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question regarding this document. I would like to know what were the circumstances and what were the reasons for which, after the war, you put those written annotations on this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was interested in knowing whether the two children I drove in my van were exchanged or not, and we came to know that they had been exchanged, indeed, and that they were alive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if we were -- if only the children were the main focus of your interest, why were you then also thinking or being preoccupied by other prisoners, after the war of course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the beginning, as I said, as we came by information, I added it to this document. Since I did not learn anything new about the others, I didn't make any annotations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I still don't understand. That information, you wanted to do what with that information, to make an investigation? Why did you need this information? I still don't understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I wasn't able to conduct an investigation. I was simply wondering about these persons. Being a human being, I was interested in knowing what their destiny was, what fate they suffered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was it was a personal interest, or was it for official purposes that you wanted to know this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a personal interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would ask that the marked version of this document be captured and admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see it's no longer marked on the screen -- I beg your pardon, I'm sorry. The marked portion of that document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number 695.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask now if the witness could be shown the document previously marked PT2501, PT2501.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you see the document on the screen in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what this document is, please?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is a regular daily combat report by the brigade commander to the division commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And which brigade commander, sir?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: 328th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could we please go to page 3 of the document in English and page 2 of the document in Bosnian, and if we could focus on paragraph 4, which is on the bottom in the Bosnian and in the middle of page 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you see paragraph 4 of this document?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you see the second bullet point or the second line under the number "4"?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you take a moment, sir, to read that to yourself, and then I'll ask you some questions about that. Have you read that, Mr. Sehic?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please comment on what's contained under the second bullet point of paragraph 4 of this document?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In his regular combat report to the Division, the commander informs them that in Kesten village, 61 enemy soldiers and three women were captured and that two children were exchanged, i.e., handed over to the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, how it was that the 328th Mountain Brigade commander had this information?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I've already told you that at the forward command post, I reported to him about everything that had transpired in Kesten, and I suppose that after that the commander drafted a written report and forwarded it, that report, to his superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And so, sir, so we're all clear, are you telling us that you were the source of this information contained in this paragraph? This was based on your oral briefing to Commander Zilkic?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I suppose so, probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, objection. I'm wondering how that witness can give the answer to that question. If he can, perhaps the witness can explain why, how he knows that he's the source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson, I've got a problem with you're objecting, and then you say, "If he can, he can explain why." What do you want him to do? Do you want him stopped from telling, or do you want him explaining how?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, from the question asked, I think it should be established whether the witness can -- is in the position to know whether he was the source of this information or whether there could have been other sources. It was put to him that, "Were you the source of this information?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, and it was because he had said, "I've already told you that I worked and made a verbal report to my commander." So he may be a source or one of the sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I withdraw the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution tenders PT2501 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: PT2501 is admitted into evidence, and may it --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just interject, this witness has been -- it has appeared previously in proceedings. I understand that it's either an MFI exhibit or it is an exhibit. I am just trying to find out what that is. I'm told it's Exhibit 480. It may be that Exhibit 480 pertained to a different PT number, but it's the same document, I'm told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I don't know. We can find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: My case manager is checking that as well, and perhaps I'll move on and then we can revisit that in just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Sehic, I would now like to turn your attention to earlier events; that is, events in January 1995. Are you familiar, sir, with a location known as "Rudine"?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us where that place is, sir?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is on the defence line of the 5th Battalion, in front of the Paljenik facility or feature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, in January 1995, what ARBiH unit, if any, was at this location?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The 5th Battalion was on that defence line, and I was its commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long did the 5th Battalion remain on the defence line at Rudine?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At Rudine, until January. In January, five or six firing points were taken over by the El Mujahid unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness now be shown the document PT1942, PT1942. And while that's coming up, my case manager has also confirmed that the previous document was, in fact, Exhibit 480 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's an MFI document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: -- which was marked as MFI, so we would go ahead and tender that into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the document then be admitted into evidence and given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will remain as Exhibit 480.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Mundis, if we can go back to the transcript, at page 42, line 7, you're asking -- I beg your pardon, line 5, you're asking the question: "How long did the 5th Battalion remain on the defence line at Rudine?" And the answer is: "At Rudine, until January. In January, five or six firing points were taken over by the El Mujahid unit." They had already been there in January, so they only stayed for the month of January. Is that the answer, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. That defence line was manned by them for some three months or so, from January to April, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you say "manned by them," who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The soldiers from the El Mujahid unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But my question to you is: Before the soldiers from the El Mujahedin Detachment came in to man that place, how long had the 5th Battalion been there? Because you told us that the 5th Battalion had been there in January, and the question by the lawyer was: "How long had the 5th Battalion remained in Rudine for, before the El Mujahid took over," if you know? If you don't know --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sehic. Mr. Mundis, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Sehic, do you see the document on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what this document is, please?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: A regular daily combat report from the 328th to the Division or - I don't know - in any case, to their superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could we please go, in the Bosnian version, to the middle half of the document, and could we please go to page 2 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Sehic, do you see, under paragraph 2, the eighth bullet point down?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This paragraph or this bullet point begins: "In the zone of responsibility of the 5th Battalion." I'm referring to that one. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what this refers to?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is an inspection of the zone of responsibility in front of the 5th Battalion in the Popovo-Osoje sector -- in the Popovo-Osoje-Rudine sector, in order to take over these firing points that I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you just tell the Trial Chamber briefly, what is referred to when you say "firing points"?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On any defence line, there are places where soldiers secure the line. Those are the so-called firing points on the defence line. They are trenches or dugouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, this part of the document makes reference to the Command of the 5th Battalion and officers from the El Mujahid Detachment made this inspection. Do you recall who from the 5th Battalion was involved in this inspection of the line?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Probably somebody from the Command. I don't remember. I wasn't there. I suppose that it was either the deputy, the -- or the assistant for Security and Intelligence, because those people were the most responsible ones for the defence line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution would ask that this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 696.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can we please show the witness document PT1943, PT1943.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. These are reports by the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please focus your attention, sir, on, again, paragraph 2, the line that begins immediately below the letters "BVG," and this is at the very bottom of the English. Do you see what I'm referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what this refers to?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I suppose this is a report by the brigade commander to his superior command, stating that the soldiers of the El Mujahid Detachment had taken over the six firing points in question towards the end of January 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution moves for this document to be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 697.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We'd ask that the witness now be shown PT2032, PT2032.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And while that document is coming up, sir, a few moments ago, in response to a question from the Presiding Judge, you told us that the El Mujahedin unit stayed at that location for a number of months. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, two or three.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you see the document on the screen in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what this document is?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could have the full view on the Bosnian version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my order for the new hand-over of the six firing points. I correct the line of defence in order to reduce the number of firing points because the El Mujahid unit had left that line of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you focus your attention, sir, on paragraph 3 of the document, and can you comment on that paragraph, please?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This means that on the 14th of April, 1995, the soldiers of the 5th Battalion or the 2nd Company of the 1st Battalion were supposed to take the defence line that had previously been manned by the El Mujahedin unit, and that this had to be carried out by 1200 hours. This means that the El Mujahedin troops had left that part of the line in order to man the line so that the line wouldn't be left unmanned. The soldiers of the 5th Battalion were supposed to take it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution asks that this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 698.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can the witness now be shown PT2086, please. PT2086.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And while that's coming up: Sir, on Thursday, as reflected on pages 5017 and 5018 of the transcript, you made reference to troops -- 30 troops directly involved in the operations Proljece and Farz 1995. Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, approximately 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you see the document on the screen in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is an order to attack from the Command of the 35th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And to whom is this document addressed?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't see the addressee of the document. I -- it was approved by the commander of the 35th Division, and it was the 328th Brigade that issued this order. It was issued by Commander Zilkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can we please go to page 2 of this document in Bosnian and page 4 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you see, sir, under paragraph 2: "Our forces," "Nasa Snaga"?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the 2nd paragraph or subparagraph under paragraph 2 refers to the 328th Mountain Brigade. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, then, if we go down to the bottom or towards the bottom of that page, we see a series of numbers. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you comment upon this part of the document, please?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHIC (Resumed)
